A mock-up is a static visual representation of a proposed interface or product. It shows the intended appearance in enough detail to discuss choices such as typography, color, spacing, imagery, and component styling.
A mock-up makes visual direction concrete for review and comparison. It can be built from a Wireframe, turning its structural outline into a more finished screen.
A mock-up communicates appearance; a clickable or responsive version may also be a prototype. The artifact's fidelity and behavior depend on what a team needs to evaluate.
A Wireframe emphasizes layout, hierarchy, and the placement of content or controls.
A mock-up emphasizes visual treatment. It may represent one screen or a set of screens without implementing their behavior.
A prototype adds behavior or interaction so people can try a proposed flow. These artifacts can be combined or revisited in different orders during design work.
Mog presents itself as a programming language for AI agents, with the public guide centered on embeddability, explicit capabilities, async host interaction, and native compilation.
Compared with mainstream application languages, Mog appears aimed less at general product development and more at constrained agent scripting and host-orchestrated workflows.

The official language guide frames Mog around a host-and-script model: the language stays relatively small while the host application provides capabilities such as I/O, HTTP, plugins, or ML operations.
This makes Mog notable less as "another general-purpose language" and more as a language design experiment for agent execution boundaries.
Capability-oriented design - Scripts declare what capabilities they require, and the guide describes those capabilities as the boundary for what code is allowed to do.
Ahead-of-time native compilation - The compiler documentation says Mog compiles to ARM64 and x86 binaries through rqbe, described there as a safe Rust implementation of the QBE backend.
Host-provided effects - The host provides capabilities and heavy operations, while the script focuses on coordination logic.
ML-adjacent data model - Mog includes tensor data structures, but the guide explicitly says the host provides the math and execution backend.
Mog programs describe behavior in the language and call into host capabilities for side effects or specialized operations.
Async capability calls are a first-class pattern in the public guide, which fits the agent and orchestration positioning.
Tensor values are built into the language as data containers, but advanced numerical work is expected to happen in the host environment.
Mog is just a tensor language -> False. Tensors are present, but the guide treats them as containers while the host performs the real computation.
Mog is a drop-in replacement for Python or JavaScript -> Not from the material I found. The official framing is much narrower and more host-driven.
Mog and Ash are direct comparables -> False. Mog is a language design for agent scripting; Ash Framework is an Elixir application framework.

A monorepo (monolithic repository) keeps many related packages, apps, or services in one version-control root instead of splitting each unit into its own repo.
Teams choose it to share CI, lint/format rules, internal libraries, and atomic cross-package changes—especially when releases must move several modules in lockstep.
Common in large product companies and open ecosystems (JS/TS with nx or GitHub/vercel/turborepo, Python workspaces, Rust workspaces, Go multi-module layouts).

Tension with multi-repo: monorepos reduce cross-repo coordination cost but raise demands on build graph performance, access control, and Dependency/Update/Automation / Software/Composition/Analysis at scale.
Workspace boundaries — Clear package names, ownership, and dependency rules so the graph stays navigable.
Task graph + caching — Incremental builds and remote cache (where available) keep CI and local dev tractable.
Policy for internal APIs — Shared libraries need semver or explicit consumer contracts so refactors do not silently break distant packages.
Workspace manifests — pnpm/yarn/npm workspaces, Poetry / uv workspace tables, Cargo workspaces, Bazel/Buck-style targets, etc., declare how packages resolve each other.
Orchestrators — Tools like nx and GitHub/vercel/turborepo schedule tasks, fan out tests, and dedupe work across the tree.
CI fan-out — Path filters, affected-only pipelines, and merge queues prevent “every push rebuilds the world” unless necessary.
One Git root shipping a mobile app, web app, and shared design-system package with a single design-token bump spanning all three.
PyPoetry/Concept/How to handle Monorepos in Poetry vs uv — language-specific packaging trade-offs inside a Python workspace.
“Monorepo = one deployable” — False; many deployables can live in one repo with separate release cadences.
“Monorepo fixes all coordination” — Oversold; you still need ownership, boundaries, and tooling discipline or the tree becomes a big ball of mud.
